nodes.label: Pattern grid painting (three-state cells)
nodes.rationale: Left paints bedrock, right paints not-bedrock, middle paints don't-care. A button per state beats cycling: painting a run of cells is one gesture instead of one to three clicks each, and dragging never has to guess what was meant. Cells are rebuilt only when the footprint changes, because recreating them mid-drag destroyed the element under the cursor and strokes came out patchy.

nodes.label: Layers store a full MAXW grid regardless of displayed size
nodes.rationale: S.w/S.h only say how much of the 16x16 store is shown, so shrinking the grid keeps what was drawn and typing '16' over '5' does not wipe four columns as it passes through '1'. setCell takes the element rather than looking it up, because the store is MAXW-strided while the DOM is S.w-strided and indexing one with the other is exactly the bug that signature makes impossible.
nodes.norm_label: layers store a full maxw grid regardless of displayed size

nodes.label: Quarter-turn rotation of the drawn pattern
nodes.rationale: One turn sends (x,z) -> (h-1-z, x) and the box from w x h to h x w. Re-basing to zero keeps every offset non-negative, so a match coordinate still names the corner of the pattern and the viewer can draw it there. The rotation lives only on the client, which also needs it for the viewer overlay, so the server just runs the pattern list it is given and the two cannot disagree.
nodes.norm_label: quarter-turn rotation of the drawn pattern

nodes.label: Self-mapping orientations are dropped, not scanned twice
nodes.rationale: A pattern with rotational symmetry maps onto itself under a turn, and scanning it again would report every match two or four times over. The binary ignores block order, so a sorted join identifies a set. A straight bar collapses to one scan at 0+180 and two at all-four; a plus sign collapses to one.
nodes.norm_label: self-mapping orientations are dropped, not scanned twice

nodes.label: Viewer overlay drawn from the searched block list
nodes.rationale: The outline is drawn from the same rotated list handed to the server rather than from the drawn grid, so it can never disagree with the orientation that actually hit. Seeing the formation on real bedrock is the point of the viewer — not trusting the number.
nodes.norm_label: viewer overlay drawn from the searched block list

nodes.label: One fluid rem unit drives the whole layout
nodes.rationale: Browser zoom does not change px sizes, it shrinks the viewport measured in CSS px, so a px-sized UI overflows as you zoom in. Sizing the root off vh with a small vw term makes the interface shrink to fit instead, and every length below is rem/em so it all follows.
nodes.norm_label: one fluid rem unit drives the whole layout

nodes.label: Half-typed input is not an instruction
nodes.source_location: web/index.html: numOf and the centre/radius handler
nodes.rationale: `+v | 0` read a half-typed field as 0 and silently wrapped anything past int32, so an out-of-range coordinate reached the server as a different number rather than as an error. Clearing a field to retype it used to read as 0 and collapse the search area to a point under the cursor, so numOf returns null and the handler declines to act.
nodes.norm_label: half-typed input is not an instruction

nodes.label: localStorage autosave of the whole editor state
nodes.rationale: Seed, grid size, layers, bounds, scan orientation, timeout and viewer position survive a reload. A quota or private-mode failure is swallowed: losing autosave is not worth a dialog.
nodes.norm_label: localstorage autosave of the whole editor state

nodes.label: The One Rule: generator must match Minecraft
nodes.rationale: The hash, xoroshiro128++ stream, splitmix64 seeding chain, per-layer probabilities and final float comparison belong to Minecraft, not the project. A finder whose RNG has drifted prints coordinates that exist in nobody's world, and does so silently, because a wrong answer is indistinguishable from a rare formation by inspection. Everything else — argument order, output format, inherited warts — is explicitly open to redesign.
nodes.norm_label: the one rule: generator must match minecraft

nodes.label: Recorded vectors replace the Java cross-check
nodes.rationale: Match counts and SHA-256 digests in tools/vectors.json were captured from a build cross-checked against the Java implementation. The project then stands on its own: no JDK, no second checkout, no network. A red gate means either the generator drifted (a bug — fix the code) or the interface changed on purpose (re-record and log a deliberate divergence); the two must never be conflated. Cases added after that cross-check record separately how they were established instead.
nodes.norm_label: recorded vectors replace the java cross-check

nodes.label: Deliberate divergences ledger
nodes.rationale: A table of knowingly-broken parity with the Java tool, so the next reader can tell intent from regression.

nodes.label: bd_hash 32-bit x vs 64-bit z asymmetry
nodes.rationale: x * 3129871 is a 32-bit multiply that wraps then sign-extends, not (long)x * 3129871L, while (long)z * 116129781L really is 64-bit. The final >> is arithmetic, not >>>. The asymmetry is deliberate and only bites past |x| ~ 686, which is why the harness tests coordinates out there. Verified load-bearing: widening the multiply fails 3 vectors, making the shift logical fails 12.

nodes.label: nextFloat stays single precision
nodes.rationale: next(24) is exactly representable in binary32 and the multiplier is exactly 2^-24, so the multiply only adjusts the exponent — it is exact, and because it is exact, widening to double and rounding back cannot change it (enumerated: 0 of 2^24 draws differ). It stays in float because that is what the generator specifies and because the exactness argument dies the moment the multiplier or shift changes. Unlike the other four internals this one needs no test: no mutation of precision alone can change a result.

nodes.label: Float comparison licensed by exhaustion, not argument
nodes.rationale: The generator specifies (double)nextFloat() < p; bd_probe compares in float. That narrowing is justified by enumerating all 2^24 draws against the four reachable probabilities rather than by reasoning. If fp_proof ever fails, bd_probe must revert to (double)f < p rather than the proof being adjusted.
nodes.norm_label: float comparison licensed by exhaustion, not argument

nodes.label: Strictness is pinned by vectors, not by fp_proof
nodes.rationale: fp_proof licenses the precision of the comparison and has no opinion on the operator. nextFloat() returns k*2^-24 and p=0.8 and p=0.6 are themselves exact multiples of 2^-24 (13421773 and 10066330), so a draw can land exactly on p; p=0.4 and p=0.2 cannot. Seed 12345 does it at (269,4168) for y=-63 and (1533,851) for y=-62. Turning < into <= looks like fixing an off-by-one, changes real output, and passed every other gate in the repo before the two float compare boundary vectors existed.
nodes.norm_label: strictness is pinned by vectors, not by fp_proof

nodes.label: The two derivers are different entry points
nodes.rationale: Step 1 runs the world seed through splitmix64; step 4 uses the two-argument constructor and does not. Routing both through one helper looks like a tidy-up and silently diverges — verified load-bearing: doing so fails 12 vectors.
nodes.norm_label: the two derivers are different entry points

nodes.label: -ffp-contract=off / --fmad=false, never --use_fast_math
nodes.rationale: The flags stop the compiler fusing start + delta * (end - start) into an FMA and changing a rounding. --use_fast_math would flush denormals and swap in approximate reciprocals, destroying bit-exactness. Unlike the other internals this one is protected by convention rather than by the harness: dropping -ffp-contract=off left all vectors passing on gcc 16 at -O2, which shows only that this compiler did not contract the expression.

nodes.label: Nether roof band is unverified against vanilla
nodes.rationale: BEDROCK_ROOF(id, 128, 128 - 5) inverts the band relative to BEDROCK_FLOOR, so y=123 is solid thinning upward to y=127 plus an always-bedrock layer at y=128. Either the Java tool got the roof wrong or that is what vanilla does; nobody has checked. Answering it requires comparing against Minecraft itself, not against this repo or the Java reference, which agree with each other by construction. Floor patterns are unaffected.
nodes.norm_label: nether roof band is unverified against vanilla

nodes.label: Missing pattern/ directory matches every column
nodes.rationale: An empty pattern makes the formation check vacuously true, so the CLI prints one line per column searched. Pure interface, inherited from Java; the web GUI already refuses it and making the CLI refuse it too is welcome.
nodes.norm_label: missing pattern/ directory matches every column

nodes.label: A test that cannot fail is not a test
nodes.rationale: Break the thing on purpose and confirm the right test fails — ideally only that one. Assert the test reaches the path it claims to: an estimate test passed for a while because its area equalled the sample budget, so the extrapolation it existed to check never ran. Assert on what the user sees, not internal state: a grid-painting bug shipped because the test read the model rather than the rendered DOM. Statistics cannot catch structural bugs; a 6% sampling bias is invisible inside a +-12% interval.
nodes.norm_label: a test that cannot fail is not a test

nodes.label: No C code in the serving path
nodes.rationale: The server shells out to the same ./gpbpf the repo builds, so the GUI can never affect the generator. The binary must only ever see integers range-checked in parse_search; never shell=True, always an argv list. python3 stdlib only, no packages, no build step, no CDN.
nodes.norm_label: no c code in the serving path

nodes.label: Measure performance, do not reason about it
nodes.rationale: Three plausible hypotheses about the kernel were wrong: the 64-bit multiplies in bd_hash were worth 6%, the div/mod unflattening the thread index was worth nothing because nvcc hoists it, and the FP64 work — assumed minor — was 67% of kernel time. Vary OMP_NUM_THREADS too; a win at 12 threads can be a loss at 1.
nodes.norm_label: measure performance, do not reason about it

nodes.label: Measured estimate instead of a probability model
nodes.rationale: Multiplying per-layer probabilities assumes independence, which holds within a layer and breaks badly across them — measured 47x low at four layers. The error is always in the direction of more matches, the unhelpful direction for a number whose job is to warn about output size, so POST /api/estimate runs the real search over a slice and extrapolates instead.
nodes.norm_label: measured estimate instead of a probability model

nodes.label: Bedrock stacks vertically more than chance
nodes.rationale: Two probes at the same column but different Y share a deriver and their hashes differ only in a few low bits before bd_hash mixes them. This is the generator's own behaviour, not a porting artefact: CPU and CUDA builds return byte-identical counts for every measured row.
nodes.norm_label: bedrock stacks vertically more than chance

nodes.label: Two-stage sampling keeps output bounded
nodes.rationale: A permissive pattern reaches its hit target in the ~260k-column first sample and stops; one that does not is by definition rare enough that the larger second sample cannot emit more than tens of thousands of lines.

nodes.label: Match rates band by Z, so the sample spans every Z
nodes.rationale: Over nine disjoint 10000x10000 tiles the spread was 2.6%, 7.8x what Poisson noise predicts, grouped almost entirely by Z — a direct consequence of bd_hash multiplying z by a full 64-bit constant while x wraps in 32 bits. A full-height strip lands within 1.6% of the true rate; a square block of the same column count was off by up to 6.1%. The reported interval combines Poisson error with a 2.5% spatial term so it never claims precision the method cannot deliver.
nodes.norm_label: match rates band by z, so the sample spans every z

nodes.label: Two vectors pin the comparison's strictness
nodes.rationale: fp_proof answers precision, not strictness. Because nextFloat() returns k*2^-24 and p=0.8 and p=0.6 are exact multiples of 2^-24, a draw can land exactly on p and < versus <= becomes observable — seed 12345 does it at (269,4168) on y=-63. Each vector window holds one such column that must stay absent plus ~100 ordinary matches, so the digest fails whichever way the comparison flips.
nodes.norm_label: two vectors pin the comparison's strictness

nodes.label: FP64 hoisted out of the kernel (67% of kernel time)
nodes.rationale: p depends only on a pattern block's y, never on (x,z), but lerpFromProgress ran inside the per-probe hot loop and contains a double-precision divide. There is no hardware FP64 divider, so nvcc emits MUFU.RCP plus Newton-Raphson DFMA, and consumer Ampere runs FP64 at 1:64. Computing it once per block on the host is bit-exact by construction; the kernel now contains zero FP64 instructions, SASS 416 -> 288.
nodes.norm_label: fp64 hoisted out of the kernel (67% of kernel time)

nodes.label: Constant-outcome blocks resolved at load time
nodes.rationale: A block outside the probabilistic bands, or with p >= 1 or p <= 0, has an outcome independent of (x,z). Contradicting the pattern makes the search provably empty; agreeing makes it redundant and it is dropped. One 20-block test went 1086 ms to 25 ms because the work was never real.
nodes.norm_label: constant-outcome blocks resolved at load time

nodes.label: Output became the bottleneck once the kernel was fast
nodes.rationale: On 4.6M matches (178 MB) wall clock went 1.13 s to 0.42 s: sort 406 -> 84 ms via an LSD radix sort over (x,z) packed into one key, and format+write 408 -> 17 ms by replacing printf and spreading formatting across the OpenMP team. Output stays byte-identical on one thread or twelve. hypot is deliberately left alone because sqrt(x*x+z*z) could change the displayed distance.
nodes.norm_label: output became the bottleneck once the kernel was fast

nodes.label: The ^0x80000000 bias makes signed order match unsigned
nodes.rationale: Without the bias a radix pass over packed (x,z) would sort negative coordinates last; one validation case compares the raw sequence across negative and positive coordinates precisely to catch that.
nodes.norm_label: the ^0x80000000 bias makes signed order match unsigned

nodes.label: CUDA is not always the fastest path
nodes.rationale: Below roughly 100M columns CUDA's ~0.2 s context initialisation costs more than the whole search and the 12-thread CPU path wins; CUDA pulls ahead on large areas. The Java original's weakest point is output rather than search — a 3.2M-match run is 10.5 s there, most of it printing.
nodes.norm_label: cuda is not always the fastest path

nodes.label: Known limits: caps reported, never silently truncated
nodes.rationale: CUDA caps the pattern at 2048 blocks (64 KB constant memory) and the match buffer at 2^24 entries, both detected and reported. Matches are buffered in memory before printing. A search spanning more than 2^63 columns is refused by CUDA and falls back to the CPU because the flattened index would not fit in long long.
nodes.norm_label: known limits: caps reported, never silently truncated

nodes.label: Web GUI for drawing patterns
nodes.rationale: Typing 25 block arguments for a 5x5 pattern is not a good time. The page draws the pattern on a grid, one tab per Y layer, and reports how selective it is before anything runs.

nodes.label: Scan more than one orientation
nodes.rationale: A pattern copied off a screenshot or video rarely comes with a reliable compass bearing. Scan chooses as-drawn, as-drawn + 180 degrees for a formation whose axis is readable but whose direction is not, or all four quarter turns. Each is a separate run of the binary merged into one result, and a pattern that maps onto itself under a turn is scanned once so a symmetric drawing does not report every match two or four times over.

nodes.label: Cancel kills the binary, not just the connection
nodes.rationale: A search holds its handler thread for as long as gpbpf runs, so the page names each request and asks POST /api/cancel to kill that name over a second connection. Dropping the request browser-side would stop the waiting and leave the GPU working.
nodes.norm_label: cancel kills the binary, not just the connection

nodes.label: Timeout is per request, not per scan
nodes.rationale: Timeout is a GUI field rather than a server flag so a scan that needs longer gets it without a restart; --timeout only sets the starting value. One deadline covers the whole request, so scanning four orientations shares it instead of taking four times as long, and a run that exceeds it says timed out rather than surfacing the SIGKILL as 'gpbpf exited -9'.
nodes.norm_label: timeout is per request, not per scan

nodes.label: Search area cap guards against a stray zero
nodes.rationale: Searches are capped at 2 billion columns (about 44,700 x 44,700) so a mistyped bound cannot turn a ten-second search into an all-day one; raise it with --max-area.
nodes.norm_label: search area cap guards against a stray zero
